en: "Only after studying Buddhism does one come to understand Confucianism. This is the discourse of a great scholar. When the ancients spoke thus, they praised it accordingly;
this was truly the impartial mind of those who were awakened first. People today do not know why the Buddha is called the Buddha, nor [do they understand] Confucianism...
The reason they are called Confucians is nothing more than their dividing themselves into separate schools and chasing after shadows while following sounds.
The World-Honored One said, "In all the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am supreme. Now tell me, what is this "I"?
The Master said, "My Way is unified by a single thread. Now tell me, what is this "one"? If one cannot clearly comprehend this very first step, one merely follows along with forms.

To discuss the traces [of the Buddha] while observing only the branches and leaves—is this not to remain outside the gate? Sages and men of profound understanding have a fundamental basis for their learning and a genuine realization of the Way.
Between the mundane and the supramundane, there has never been any duality; in awakening oneself and awakening others, there is no distinction whatsoever.
He may manifest as a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā; or he may manifest as a high official, a householder, a brāhmaṇa, or a lay devotee.
According to the convergence of conditions, wherever he goes, he guides and benefits all classes of beings, establishing a model for future generations.
This is what is meant by being "one who has awakened first. Through a single faculty, a single object, a single conversation, or a single word, he can open up and reveal the truth.
The Correct Eye of Humans and Devas, which elucidates the heart-essence of both Confucianism and Buddhism, is the reason for the compilation of the *Xianjue ji* (Anthology of the Enlightened).

Regarding the fact that Master Qiantao of the Ming dynasty compiled the *Xianjue ji* yet retained only the section on Laymen (*Jushi*), it was because he established a Vimalakīrti Hall to provide a seat for him;
thus, he examined the origins of his entry into the Way, whereby he [was seen to] share [a lineage] with Master Yunju and others.

O friends on the Way, you have deliberated and verified [the texts] to bring these words to completion. Although they are not yet entirely exhaustive, they already reveal a significant portion [of the truth].
Your merit is truly great! Since the general purport has already been proclaimed in the inscription for the Zhongshan stele, this collection is now being carved upon woodblocks;
I am thus asked to provide a preface and further clarify its teachings.
Written by the monk Dao Anjing, the thirty-second generation successor of the Linji Orthodox Lineage,
in the sixth month of summer in the year Jiwu (1679) of the Kangxi era.
Preface to the *Collection of Preceding Awakenings*:
From the time of antiquity until now, the Buddhas, patriarchs, sages, and various bodhisattvas have expounded all manner of dharmas and propagated all manner of teachings;
yet these are all like smoke and dust in a mirror, or illusory events in a dream. Fundamentally, there is no real dharma that binds or attaches itself to people. Therefore—
"The Way of the Great Awakened World-Honored One: for forty-nine years, I have never spoken a single word.
This is a true statement. Furthermore, an ancient said: "The great trichiliocosm is but a bubble on the sea; all sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning.
Herein, where has there ever been a Buddha, a Dharma, a monk, or a layperson? Where is there awakening or non-awakening? It is not seen that one has departed from the Tuṣita Heaven.

Śūratāra had already descended into the royal palace, yet before he had even emerged from his mother’s womb, his work of delivering sentient beings was complete. This is the profound record of the Primordial Awakened One (Sengcan).
Tao Mingqian understood this meaning and compiled the *Xianjue ji* (Anthology of the Primordial Awakened One), wishing to circulate it in the world. He requested a preface from me.

I, having overturned the ancient sharp-pointed tools [of scholarship] in a single stroke, offer this view for those who have attained realization; for those who have not yet realized it, they must strictly avoid [such conceptualization].
Stumbling toward the assembly of those who have realized awakening.
Written on the day the Buddha attained enlightenment in the Bingyin year of the Kangxi era by Zhipu of Qinggou at Panshan.
Preface to the *Collection of the Awakened* (Xianjue ji):
The Way of succeeding Heaven and establishing the Ultimate Pole is no different from Chan; the books that transmit the world and establish the teaching all converge upon Principle (*li*).
The Way is not manifest without words, and Principle is not clarified without phenomena. Thus, among the Confucians, there are the *Fen*, *Dian*, and the Classics.
The histories, the various schools of thought, and even the unofficial records and vernacular tales—each has its own fundamental tenets.

Only in our Buddhist tradition do we find the texts from the Western Heaven and the Eastern Land, the principles of the Northern Teaching and the Southern School, the collateral streams and the direct lineages, and the various branches and distinct sects.
Through the profound sources of transmission and reception, the written records have fortunately been preserved; thus, there is sufficient evidence for verifying the facts.

The transmission of the lamp has been disordered and the succession to the seat has been fraught with error. This serves to further confirm that all linguistic expressions are the *samādhi* of the threefold world;

thus, the collections of both internal (Buddhist) and external (secular) classics are all vessels for carrying the Way and instruments for transmitting it to posterity. Their merit in benefiting future generations is by no means small.

Herein lies the lay practitioner Ming Qiantao, who has studied for many years and labored for a very long time. Through diligent inquiry and earnest investigation, he has traversed every path of bitter toil.
Suan crossed rivers and climbed mountains, thoroughly understanding their cold and warmth. In the winter of the *renzi* year, he suddenly attained realization within the chamber of Haihui.
Shortly thereafter, he took his leave to go to Zhongshan Temple, where he cleared weeds and tilled the clouds, sitting in the lotus posture amidst the shadows of the gate, hearing no worldly affairs.

He further examined the remaining fragments of texts and subsequently compiled the *Xianjue ji* (Collection of the Formerly Enlightened) in two volumes, arranging the accounts of the laymen (*upāsaka*) and laywomen (*upāsikā*) from the masters above.
"Gentlemen, you have requested that I provide a preface to assist [this work]. Unconsciously, I am moved to a deep sigh.

To preach the Dharma in the body of a layman (jushi) and to offer worship likewise in the body of a layman—when one considers the Patriarch’s coming from the West, how many such instances of offering can there be?

Only then do we know that the manifestation of the True Teaching depends entirely upon the person; if it is not the right person, one cannot propagate the Way, and if it is not the right Way, [it cannot be propagated]."
To be able to know such a person, whose name and reality are fully perfected throughout the world—who else but a Perfected Person (zhiren) could achieve this?

However, regarding the task of compiling records and chronicling events, if one does not thoroughly investigate the subtleties of the principles of the Buddhas and the Enlightened Ones, and fails to prune and supplement the difficult passages to avoid omissions, then the perspective of the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) will instead incur the reproach of being like "auspicious grass in the courtyard. As for all of us...

Fellow practitioners, you must surely embrace the unobstructed contemplation. Upon contemplating it, you will immediately know that the ten ages of past and present do not depart from the present moment.

As for the arising and ceasing of dust-like shadows, what is there to record? Naturally, when one lifts the eyes to look, all desires are fulfilled; when one reaches out the hand to grasp, all ailments are healed.

Laypeople and monastics alike gaze upon this together, and its fame is broadcast throughout renowned monasteries. Thus, the sages of old are no longer solitary, and the late assembly may indeed be considered complete.
A trust. This is a truly sublime matter. Therefore, I venture to take up paper and wield my brush, offering this brief exhortation for the sake of the blue-eyed iron man.
At this time.
Composed by Yuanjiao Jiesan on an auspicious day in the spring of the Dingmao year of the Kangxi era.
